title: T-Mobile illegally imposed 50GB cap on low-income home Internet plan, NY says
gist: New York says T-Mobile violated the Affordable Broadband Act by capping low-income fixed-wireless plans at 50GB/month then throttling to 600 Kbps, limiting them to 5G areas, and hiding the plan page from search; T-Mobile settled without admitting wrongdoing. Separately it settled over breaking lifetime price-guarantee promises, while Trump-administration BEAD preemption claims could revive industry challenges to state broadband price rules.

themes.theme: T-Mobile ABA violations and settlement terms

insights.claim: New York alleged T-Mobile capped its low-income fixed wireless home Internet plans at 50GB per month and then cut download speeds from 25 Mbps to 600 Kbps, which a typical customer could hit after about four days.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Shows how carriers engineered low-income mandated plans to limit cost, now curtailed by regulators.
insights.quote: “a typical customer could hit the data cap after about four days of usage.”

insights.claim: T-Mobile offered New York's mandated low-income plans only in 5G home Internet areas even though it sold full-price 25 Mbps plans in 4G areas, and coded its plan webpage to block search-engine indexing.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Regulators are scrutinizing dark patterns and availability gating in subsidized offerings.

insights.claim: Under the settlement T-Mobile must remove the data and speed limits, extend low-income plans to every address where it offers residential fixed wireless (including 4G areas), and stop noindexing the plan page, within 120 days.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Raises cost-to-serve of T-Mobile's low-income fixed wireless base in New York.

insights.claim: T-Mobile offers 5G home Internet to roughly 40 percent of homes in rural upstate New York and 4G LTE home Internet to the rest of its fixed wireless footprint there.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Extension to 4G areas could materially expand eligible low-income plan footprint upstate.

insights.claim: The settlement exempts speed reductions caused solely by network congestion and allows sub-25 Mbps speeds where T-Mobile couldn't deliver 25 Mbps to a regular customer at the same address.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Leaves carriers operational flexibility, limiting financial impact of compliance.

insights.claim: T-Mobile neither admitted nor denied the New York Attorney General's findings in the settlement.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Limits precedent and liability spillover for T-Mobile in other jurisdictions.

insights.claim: New York's Affordable Broadband Act lets the attorney general sue providers for restitution and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Per-violation penalties can scale with customer counts if a carrier breaches the settlement.

themes.theme: Affordable Broadband Act mechanics and legal history

insights.claim: New York's Affordable Broadband Act requires home Internet providers with at least 20,000 customers to offer income-eligible households broadband at $15 per month for at least 25 Mbps or $20 per month for at least 200 Mbps.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: State price regulation caps revenue on a segment of ISP subscribers.

insights.claim: New York began enforcing the Affordable Broadband Act in January 2025 after a nearly four-year court fight against broadband lobby groups including CTIA, taking effect a month after the Supreme Court rejected the industry's challenge.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Validated state-level broadband price regulation could be copied by other states.

insights.claim: Cable company Optimum failed to comply with the ABA shortly after it took effect, twice rejecting an eligible low-income customer until Ars inquired.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Compliance gaps across ISPs suggest further enforcement risk.

insights.claim: New York took almost 18 months to investigate T-Mobile's compliance, starting after the Department of Public Service raised concerns in June 2025.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Enforcement timelines are slow, implying long lag between violation and remedy.

insights.claim: The Trump administration asserts that states must not enforce price regulations or net neutrality laws against any ISP receiving grants from the $42 billion BEAD program, which could aid future ISP challenges to New York's law; California disputes this preemption authority.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Federal preemption could neutralize state broadband price caps, a key regulatory swing factor for ISPs.

insights.claim: New York found T-Mobile raised prices by about $5 per line in 2024 on 2017–2019 'Price Guarantee Plans' that promised to never change the price, affecting about 252,957 plans in New York.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Legacy price-lock repricing is a regulatory liability for carriers seeking ARPU growth.
insights.quote: promising to ‘never change the price you pay,’

insights.claim: T-Mobile agreed to reimbursement options and a price lock until May 2029 valued by the AG at up to $38 million, plus a $98,834.75 fine, though T-Mobile says the $38 million is an estimate of optional benefits rather than payments.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Actual cash cost to T-Mobile is likely far below the headline figure.
insights.quote: “The $38 million cited in the press release is an estimate of potential benefits that a group of long-standing T-Mobile customers may choose to take advantage of, not the amount in refunds or payments,”
